content:
Over the past few days, there have been two reports suggesting different ways Apple is looking to increase profits by growing services revenue.

I think Apple absolutely should pursue the first approach, but not the second — and it looks like Phil Schiller may well agree…

First, let's recap those two reports.

Home security and monitoring service

On Friday, Bloomberg reported that Apple may be planning to launch an entirely new home security and monitoring service, alongside some of the new home hardware we expect it to introduce.

Squeezing more from the App Store

The same source reported on Sunday that the company is looking at ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple should NOT take the latter approach

Taking the two suggestions in reverse order, I think the second one would be a very serious mistake.

Apple's de facto monopoly on iPhone app sales has come under attack from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell apps for iPhone, you have to do so through the official App Store, leaving you with no choice but to accept Apple's terms on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.

I know the general view is that no one is forced to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but that's not how laissez-faire capitalism actually works in practice: the US has had antitrust laws since 1890. When you reach a certain level of market dominance, your behavior is constrained to ensure you don't abuse that position.

Trying to squeeze more money from the App Store is the very opposite of 'skating to where the puck is headed.' According to Bloomberg, Phil Schiller shares this view, and says it's one of the reasons for his stepping down now.

Innovative services is the right direction

Launching innovative services that people are happy to pay for is, by contrast, absolutely something Apple should be doing. I can easily see the value of the company offering a home security monitoring service.

I argued back in 2024 that designing its own smart home cameras would be one of the … smartest moves the company could make. I've expressed the same view regarding rumored Apple smart doorbells. Adding an optional service bundle to security products has two great benefits, which makes perfect sense.

First, it ties in with the various privacy arguments I've made over the years. The HomeKit Secure Video feature already does a great deal to ensure the privacy of security camera footage. If I were to choose a company I trusted to analyze my security camera footage with AI, it would be Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best placed to integrate security hardware and services fully within the HomeKit ecosystem. I believe Apple could offer similar benefits in many other areas as well.

For me, the key is that Apple needs to treat services with the same attitude it brings to hardware — building great products people willingly and happily pay for, rather than extracting money in ways that infuriate customers, developers, and regulators.

What are your thoughts? Feel free to share them in the comments.
